parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A father phones a leisure centre about swimming lessons for his daughter.
script: Good morning, Brook Leisure Centre, Kelly speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book swimming lessons for my daughter.
Ama Osei. The surname is O, S, E, I.
She can float on her back, and she's not afraid of the water, but she can't really swim yet.
Then she'd go into our Dolphins group. The Ducklings group is for children who aren't confident in the water yet.
Dolphins sounds right. When are the lessons?
There's a group on Wednesday afternoons, but it's full. There's space on Saturday mornings at ten fifteen.
Good. The course runs for ten weeks and costs sixty-five pounds in total.
Does she need any special equipment?
Just a swimming cap. It's required for all children with longer hair, and we ask everyone to wear one.
Yes, from the balcony above the pool. Parents aren't allowed on the poolside, I'm afraid.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide introduces a transport museum.
script: Good morning, and welcome to the City Transport Museum. My name's Anna, and I'm going to tell you a little about the museum before you look around.
The museum opened in 1995 in this building, which was originally a tram depot, where the city's trams were repaired and stored at night. You can still see the rails in the floor.
Our most popular exhibit with children is the flight simulator on the first floor, where they can try to land a plane. There's often a queue, so I'd go early.
Guided tours run at eleven and three, and they're free. You don't need to book; just meet at the information desk.
Our café is on the roof, with great views over the river, and it's open until half past four.
Let me mention a few of our star exhibits. The horse-drawn coach in the main hall was used by the royal family when they visited the city in the nineteenth century.
Next to it is the steam locomotive called Victory. It's been fully restored, and it still works. On special days in summer, it pulls a short train along our outdoor track.
The penny-farthing bicycle, from 1872, is the oldest object in the museum.
Visitors are welcome to climb aboard tram number seven and sit in the driver's seat. It's a great place for photos.
The red racing car spent fifty years in a private collection in Argentina before the museum bought it back in 2019.
And finally, the fire engine near the exit was built here in the city, at a factory that closed in the 1960s.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Leo, discusses his business plan with his tutor, Dr Patel.
script: Leo, I've read your business plan for the food truck. It's an interesting idea.
Thank you. It's based on my grandmother's recipes. She used to cook Bangladeshi street food, and I've always wanted to share it.
That gives the business a real story. Now, you plan to park outside the university library?
Yes, that's where most students pass.
The location makes sense, but you haven't mentioned the licence. You'll need permission from the council to trade there, and that can take months.
I didn't realise. I'll look into it.
Your market research survey had two hundred responses, which is good. But you only sent it to your friends and their friends, so the results may be biased.
That's true. I'll try to reach a wider group.
Also, I think your prices are too low. At those prices, you wouldn't cover the cost of ingredients and fuel.
Students will pay a fair price for good food. And for funding, have you thought about the university's start-up grant? It's designed for student businesses.
Let's go through the sections. The executive summary is too long. It should be one page, not three.
Your market analysis is very clear. I wouldn't change it.
Good. What about the financial forecast?
It's unrealistic. You're predicting profits in the first month, which almost never happens.
The ideas are fine, but you need more detail, for example on costs and timing. And you haven't included a risk assessment at all.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of printing.
script: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at the history of printing, which many historians consider one of the most important inventions of all time.
Printing began in East Asia, not in Europe. The oldest surviving printed book with a date is a Buddhist text, the Diamond Sutra, printed in China in the year 868, using carved wooden blocks.

Woodblock printing was slow, because a new block had to be carved for every page. In the eleventh century, a Chinese inventor named Bi Sheng created movable type, individual characters made of clay that could be arranged and reused. In Korea, printers later developed movable type made of metal.

In Europe, the key figure is Johannes Gutenberg, who developed his printing system around 1450 in the German city of Mainz. Gutenberg had trained as a goldsmith, which gave him the metalworking skills to produce large numbers of identical metal letters.

He also developed a new ink based on oil, which stuck to metal type far better than the water-based inks used for woodblocks. And his press was adapted from the machines that were used to press grapes when making wine.
His most famous product, the Gutenberg Bible, was printed in about one hundred and eighty copies, a remarkable number at the time.
The technology spread with astonishing speed. By 1500, there were printing presses in more than two hundred European cities, and historians estimate that around twenty million books had been printed.

The consequences were enormous. Printing made books cheaper, encouraged literacy and allowed ideas to spread quickly. It played a crucial role in the Reformation, when religious pamphlets were printed and distributed in huge numbers.

passages.title: The Grain That Feeds the World
paragraphs: Rice is the staple food for more than half of the world's population, providing a large share of daily calories for billions of people in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Asian rice was domesticated around 9,000 years ago in the valley of the Yangtze River in China. African rice is a separate species, domesticated independently in West Africa about 3,000 years ago.

Unlike most crops, rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies. The plant can survive in standing water, but most weeds cannot, so flooding is an effective way of controlling them. It also helps to keep soil temperatures stable. In mountainous regions, farmers have carved terraces into hillsides to create flat, flooded fields. The rice terraces of Banaue in the Philippines, built by the Ifugao people around 2,000 years ago, are among the most spectacular examples and are recognised by UNESCO.

In the 1960s, many experts feared that Asia faced widespread famine, as populations were growing faster than food production. Part of the solution came from the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, which in 1966 released a new variety called IR8. It had short, strong stems that could support heavy heads of grain without falling over, and when grown with fertiliser and irrigation, it produced far higher yields than traditional varieties. Nicknamed 'miracle rice', it became a symbol of the Green Revolution.

Rice cultivation does, however, have an environmental cost. When fields are flooded, bacteria in the waterlogged soil produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Rice paddies are responsible for around one-tenth of the methane released by human activity. Rice also requires very large amounts of water.

Researchers have developed methods to reduce these problems. In a technique called alternate wetting and drying, farmers allow fields to dry out periodically instead of keeping them permanently flooded. Studies have found that this can reduce water use by around 30 percent and cut methane emissions significantly, without lowering yields.

Scientists are also trying to improve rice's nutritional value. Golden rice has been genetically modified to contain beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. Vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and weakens the immune system in millions of children. After many years of controversy, the Philippines approved golden rice for cultivation in 2021, although its use has faced legal challenges.

passages.title: Into the Deep
paragraphs: It is often said that we know more about the surface of the Moon than about the floor of our own oceans. The deep sea, usually defined as water below 200 metres, where sunlight begins to fade, makes up the great majority of the living space on Earth. Yet only a tiny fraction of it has ever been directly observed.

One of the most important discoveries in the history of biology was made there. In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin were exploring the Galápagos Rift in the Pacific when they found hydrothermal vents, cracks in the seabed releasing hot, mineral-rich water. Around them lived communities of giant tube worms, clams and crabs. These ecosystems did not depend on sunlight at all. Instead, bacteria used chemicals from the vents to produce energy, a process called chemosynthesis.

Deep-sea animals have evolved extraordinary adaptations. Many produce their own light, a phenomenon called bioluminescence. A study of observations off the coast of California found that around three-quarters of the animals recorded could produce light, which they use to attract prey, find mates or confuse predators. The anglerfish, for example, dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth.

Exploring these depths requires remarkable technology. In 1960, two men in the bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean, at almost 11,000 metres. Today, most deep-sea research is carried out by remotely operated vehicles, controlled by cable from a ship, and by autonomous robots that can explore on their own for days at a time.

The deep sea is also attracting commercial interest. Large areas of the seabed, particularly the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific, are covered with potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules, which contain metals such as nickel, cobalt and manganese that are used in batteries. Mining companies are keen to collect them, but scientists warn that mining could destroy habitats that took millions of years to form, and the International Seabed Authority has not yet agreed rules for commercial extraction.

Part of the concern is how little we know about what lives there. A study published in 2023 estimated that the Clarion-Clipperton Zone alone is home to around 5,000 species, of which roughly nine out of ten have never been described by science. Many researchers argue that mining should not begin until we understand these ecosystems far better.

passages.title: Can Money Buy Happiness?
paragraphs: The relationship between money and happiness has puzzled economists and psychologists for decades. In 1974, the economist Richard Easterlin observed a strange pattern. Within any single country, richer people tended to report being happier than poorer people. Yet as countries became richer over time, average happiness did not seem to rise. This apparent contradiction became known as the Easterlin paradox.

One influential attempt to explain it came in 2010, when the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton analysed survey data from hundreds of thousands of Americans. They concluded that people's day-to-day emotional wellbeing increased with income only up to around $75,000 a year, after which it levelled off. The figure was widely reported, and many people concluded that, beyond a certain point, more money makes no difference.

Later research has complicated this picture. In 2021, the psychologist Matthew Killingsworth, using data collected through a smartphone app, found that wellbeing continued to rise with income well beyond $75,000. Rather than simply argue, Kahneman and Killingsworth then worked together to re-examine the data. Their joint study, published in 2023, concluded that for most people happiness keeps rising with income, and that a plateau appears only among the least happy group, whose unhappiness may have causes that money cannot fix.

Other research suggests that how people spend money matters as much as how much they have. Studies by the psychologists Leaf Van Boven and Thomas Gilovich found that spending on experiences, such as travel or concerts, tends to produce more lasting happiness than spending on possessions, partly because experiences become part of our identity and are less likely to be compared with what others have. In a well-known experiment, Elizabeth Dunn and her colleagues gave people small sums of money and told some to spend it on themselves and others to spend it on someone else. Those who spent it on others reported feeling happier at the end of the day.

Time also matters. Research led by Ashley Whillans found that people who paid for services that saved them time, such as cleaning or delivery, reported greater life satisfaction, because it freed them from disliked tasks and gave them time for activities they enjoyed. Comparison, on the other hand, can reduce the benefits of wealth: a pay rise feels less satisfying if colleagues receive more.

In my view, it would be wrong to conclude that money does not matter. For people on low incomes, more money can transform their lives, reducing stress and improving health and security. But for those whose basic needs are met, the evidence suggests that how money is spent, on experiences, on other people and on time, matters at least as much as how much of it we have.

task1.text: The table below shows the number of students, in thousands, enrolled in five university subjects in one country in 2005, 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table shows how many students were enrolled in engineering, medicine, business, arts and computer science at universities in one country in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

Overall, enrolment rose in four of the five subjects, with computer science showing by far the most dramatic growth. Arts was the only subject to decline, while business remained the most popular subject throughout, despite a slight fall after 2015.

In 2005, business attracted the most students, at 150,000, followed by engineering with 120,000 and arts with 110,000. Medicine and computer science were much smaller, with 60,000 and 40,000 students respectively.

Over the next twenty years, computer science enrolment more than quadrupled to 170,000, making it the second most popular subject by 2025, only slightly behind business at 180,000. Engineering and medicine grew steadily, reaching 150,000 and 85,000. In contrast, the number of arts students fell continuously, from 110,000 to 70,000, so that by 2025 arts had become the least popular of the five subjects.

task2.text: Some people think that it is better for children to grow up in the countryside, while others believe that a city is a better place for children. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Where a child grows up can shape their health, education and opportunities. While some people believe that the countryside offers the best environment for children, others argue that cities provide more advantages. In my view, both have important strengths, but a city generally offers children more opportunities, especially as they grow older.

Those who prefer the countryside emphasise health and freedom. Rural areas usually have cleaner air, less traffic and more open space, so children can play outdoors, explore nature and develop independence in a relatively safe environment. Communities are often smaller and closer, which can give children a strong sense of belonging. In addition, rural life may protect children from some of the pressures of city life, such as crime and constant consumerism.

On the other hand, cities offer access to a much wider range of opportunities. Urban schools often have more resources and offer more subjects and activities, and there is easier access to libraries, museums, sports clubs and specialist healthcare. Children growing up in cities also meet people from many different backgrounds, which can make them more open-minded and better prepared for the diverse world of work. For teenagers in particular, the limited options for education and leisure in rural areas can be frustrating.

In my opinion, the advantages of the city are greater, particularly for older children, because education and exposure to different ideas have a lasting effect on their future. However, city families should make a conscious effort to give children time outdoors and in nature, for example through parks and weekend trips.
In conclusion, while the countryside offers health and freedom, I believe cities provide richer opportunities that better prepare children for adult life.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you were late for something important.
You should say:
- what you were late for
- why you were late
- what happened as a result
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about the time I was late for an important university exam in my first year. It was my first final exam, a mathematics paper, and it started at nine in the morning. I'd set two alarms, but there was a power cut during the night, and my phone, which was charging, ran out of battery. So neither alarm went off. I woke up at eight fifteen, which would normally be fine, but it was raining heavily, and Dhaka traffic in the rain is famously terrible. I jumped into a rickshaw, then got stuck in a huge traffic jam, and in the end I ran the last kilometre in the rain. I arrived about twenty minutes late, completely soaked. Luckily, the rules allowed students to enter up to thirty minutes after the start, so I was allowed in, but I didn't get any extra time. I was so stressed for the first part of the exam that I couldn't think clearly, and I didn't finish the last question. I still passed, but with a lower grade than I'd hoped. I felt really frustrated, mainly with myself. Since then, I always keep a small battery-powered alarm clock, and I leave much earlier than I need to for anything important.
